div.p: After recapitulating, in Chapter 1, the Journalistic treatment and Legal ramifications of the Cornell 7 case, we engaged in a brief modern history sketch of the underlying phenomenon in Chapter 2 and attempted a structural analysis of its psychological foundations with the help of René Girard's anthropology of Desire in Chapter 3. We are now beginning a more in-depth dive into the longue dureé historical development of the family of cultural-religious phenomena to which frat ritual sex belongs. In doing so, we will be forced to break a certain number of Academic taboos, the collective existence of which explains why such an overdue work has not been attempted yet. We have become accustomed to the steady stream of Academic scandals that have emerged in recent years: fraud, plagiarism, the recruitment of obviously unsuitable individuals, etc. Yet, we should not forget that the biggest scandal of all is the increasing refusal of Academia to say anything at all; to risk synthesis and comparison in the service of better overall understanding. Our position outside of Academia enables us to undertake such a work without fear of institutional retribution.

div.head: 4.1. Hammurabi and his Roman counterpart
div.p: Hammurabi of Babylon represents a paradigmatic early example of a sovereign who systematically deployed the righteous ruler persona. He erected the stelae bearing his famous code of law—functioning less as a strictly operational legal code in the modern sense and more as a monumental advertisement of his commitment to cosmic justice—and he extended generous patronage to protective deities associated with righteousness and order, such as Shamash (depicted on the stele itself) and Marduk (the paternal poliad god of Babylon). Concurrently, however, his annual participation in the Akitu festival served to confirm his martial-erotic fitness to rule, a status conferred by the goddess Inanna-Ishtar through the hieros gamos ceremony. While the Apollonian dimension of his rule is pronounced, it was critically offset by a frankly DionysianWe use these terms here only in a suggestive manner and will discard them later on. We are certainly not employing them in their strict Nietzschean sense. See Friedrich Nietzsche, The Birth of Tragedy (Leipzig: E. W. Fritzsch, 1872). component. The historical record suggests that the actualization of his legitimacy relied disproportionately upon the latter. One might characterize this ideological framework as an Ishtarian fist concealed within a glove of righteousnessThis expression is a deliberate adaptation of the Legalist fist in a Confucian glove metaphor from Chinese historiography. Although the two sets of concepts are not historically analogous, the fist-and-glove metaphor effectively captures the dynamic of power justification described here..

Nearly two millennia later in Rome, Augustus legitimized the dismantling of the Roman Republican constitutional order through a strikingly homologous mechanism. He systematically projected an aura of Apollonian righteousness, emphasized symbolic deference to the Senate, and governed under the ostensibly modest title of princeps. Fundamentally, however, the material basis of his supremacy rested upon the loyalty of the legions bequeathed to him by his adoptive father, Caesar, the nominal descendant of Venus. Here, the same structural dynamic is evident: an Ishtarian (Venus) fist concealed within a glove of righteousness (Apollo). The Apollonian archetype is frequently contrasted with the Dionysian, but structural analysis reveals the more historically salient dichotomy to be Apollo/Venus (Marduk/Ishtar) rather than the traditional Apollo/Dionysos binary. While Mark Antony conspicuously emphasized his Dionysian associations, this served primarily as a vector for a hyper-Venusian (Ishtarian) political theology. Augustus required no such overt displays; he successfully galvanized the devotion of the army without resorting to explicit ecstatic performance.

The earliest archaeologically attested instantiation of this bifurcated system of sovereignty justification is located in the dual sacred precincts of the Late Chalcolithic (fourth millennium BCE) city of Uruk in Southern Mesopotamia. The western precinct, Kullaba, was dedicated to Anu, the sky god and archetype of the aforementioned righteous, paternal deities. The eastern precinct, E-Anna, served as the cultic center for the goddess Inanna, the Sumerian predecessor of the Akkadian-Babylonian Ishtar. Extant sources from the latter half of the third millennium BCE onward provide incontrovertible evidence of this goddess's formidable martial-erotic pedigree. Consider, for example, the following passages:

cit.quote: When I sit by the gate of the tavern, I am a prostitute familiar with the penis; the friend of a man, the girlfriend of a woman.
cit.bibl: Jeremy Black, Graham Cunningham, Eleanor Robson, and Gábor Zólyomi, A cir-namcub to Inana (Inana I), in The Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature (Oxford: University of Oxford, 1998), lines 16-22.

cit.quote: Goddess of the fearsome divine powers, clad in terror, riding on the great divine powers, Inanna, made complete by the strength of the holy ankar weapon, drenched in blood, rushing around in great battles, with shield resting on the ground, covered in storm and flood...
cit.bibl: Jeremy Black, Graham Cunningham, Eleanor Robson, and Gábor Zólyomi, Inana and Ebiḫ, in The Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature (Oxford: University of Oxford, 1998), lines 1-4.

div.p: By this period, Anu had evidently transitioned into the structural role of a deus otiosus:

cit.quote: Anu is the father and king of the gods... but he is a deus otiosus, an aloof god who has withdrawn to the highest heavens.
cit.bibl: Thorkild Jacobsen, The Treasures of Darkness: A History of Mesopotamian Religion (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1976), p. 95.

div.p: Nonetheless, both archaeological stratigraphy and later mythological traditions point to an intense institutional rivalryThis rivalry is vividly dramatized in the Sumerian poem Gilgamesh and the Bull of Heaven, where Inanna intimidates Anu into giving her the Bull of Heaven by demanding: Give me the Bull of Heaven or I will shout, and make my voice reach heaven and earth! See Jeremy Black, Graham Cunningham, Eleanor Robson, and Gábor Zólyomi, Gilgameš and the Bull of Heaven, in The Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature (Oxford: University of Oxford, 1998), lines 46-51. between the factions affiliated with the two precincts in Late Chalcolithic Uruk. The Anu Ziggurat in the Kullaba underwent successive monumental reconstructions to project its dominance over the urban skyline, while the E-Anna precinct horizontally expanded into a vast administrative and cultic complex. It is highly probable that the Kullaba faction was directed by a predecessor of the ensi (the civic governor-administrator of later epochs), whereas the E-Anna was commanded by a proto-monarch of the lugal classification. Regardless of exact titles, it remains unclear whether this early friction ever crystallized into the institutionalized dualism later perfected by Hammurabi or Augustus. Periodically, the friction between the Kullaba and E-Anna factions in Late Chalcolithic Uruk likely resembled the overtly adversarial dynamic of the civil war between Octavian (Kullaba) and Mark Antony (E-Anna) rather than the classical Babylonian synthesis.

In the late third millennium BCE, Sargon of Akkad's dynasty successfully governed the Mesopotamian basin briefly by relying almost exclusively upon E-Anna martial-erotic spirit, whereas his imperial successors, the Third Dynasty of Ur, pivoted to an intensely Kullaba-centric administrative model (pioneering the structural antecedents of Hammurabi's code). A durably stable synthesis of these competing engines was not truly formalized until the early second millennium BCE.

The bipartite architecture of state administration and ideological legitimation delineated so far constitutes what we will term the Kullaba/E-Anna model—or, interchangeably, the Anu/Ishtar or Anu/Inanna paradigm. As demonstrated, this framework can manifest either as a highly stable, institutionalized quasi-constitution (Hammurabi, Augustus) or as a volatile structural antagonism bordering on civil collapse (the Late Chalcolithic Uruk precincts in times of crisis, Octavian versus Mark Antony). The historical oscillation between these two modalities is an inherent feature of the model.

div.head: 4.2. The Girardian mechanics on both sides
div.p: The operational mechanics of the E-Anna faction are, once again, best elucidated through the theoretical framework of Girardian mimetic desire we have already used in the previous chapter. Within this relational architecture, the goddess functions as the mediator, actively broadcasting her divine desire for the sovereign. The sovereign consequently becomes the hyper-valorized object of desire, while the populace occupies the role of desiring subjects, unconsciously imitating the mediator's passion. By channeling her divine, erotic passion toward the monarch, the goddess precipitates his mimetic elevation to a semi-divine status. This sociopsychological dynamic constitutes the bedrock of what historiography has conventionally termed Oriental DespotismWe are well aware that Oriental Despotism has become a colonialist dirty word in modern scholarship. Yet the very fact that it exists demonstrates that observers had realized something akin to the dynamic described here existed. See Karl A. Wittfogel, Oriental Despotism: A Comparative Study of Total Power (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1957).—a structural paradigm wherein the ruler is ideologically insulated from the profane sphere.

This triangular mimetic architecture accounts for the remarkable ideological potency and cross-cultural diffusionWe are keenly aware that this macro-historical framework invites accusations of hyperdiffusionism. We unapologetically maintain, however, that tracing these structural homologies across vast spans of time and geography is analytically essential, and we reject the dogma of absolute regional isolationism which infects current historiography. of the Ishtarian paradigm. Because mimetic desire operates as a highly contagious psychosocial mechanism, the goddess's localized favor for the king swiftly metastasizes throughout the populace, forging a formidable engine of mass devotion and centralized charismatic authority. However, this engine is inherently volatile. The mimetic escalation catalyzed by the E-Anna precinct perpetually threatens to breach its structural constraints, risking a descent into chaotic factional violence and societal implosion. Consequently, the Kullaba apparatus—embodying law, bureaucratic rationality, and Apollonian order—is engaged in a permanent structural imperative to contain, quantify, and redirect this explosive energy. Indeed, major phases of political evolution can be analyzed as successive attempts by Kullaba-aligned institutions to subjugate the volatile charismatic surplus of the E-Anna, a dialectic mapped in the subsequent table.

While the mimetic dynamic is most conspicuously at work on the E-Anna side of the equation, it is simultaneously operationalized by the Kullaba. In this parallel sphere, the object of desire is the paternal cosmic deity (Anu, Marduk, Shamash), and the initial catalyst of desire is supplied by the bureaucratic priesthood initiating orthopraxic rituals. By adopting a posture of ritual prostration, the clerisy assumes the role of the little children of the GospelMatthew 18:3-4: Truly I say to you, unless you change and become like little children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. soliciting paternal protection. This institutionalized deference is subsequently imitated by the broader population, synthesizing a coalition of the meek endowed with sufficient structural gravity to serve as a thermodynamic regulator against the potentially destabilizing, hyper-masculine energies of the E-Anna.

Mimetic loops are operating on both sides of the sovereignty divide. As Jean-Pierre Dupuy—from whom we derive the term mimetic loop—has demonstrated, such mechanisms become self-reinforcing circuits of desire and imitation.See Jean-Pierre Dupuy, The Mark of the Sacred (Stanford: Stanford University Press, 2013). In the case of the Kullaba, the loop is manifested as more and more frightened but mimetically attracted people come and prostrate before the paternal deity (c.f. mass street prayers in Islam). On the E-Anna side, the engine of the mimetic loop is the orgiastic thiasus or warband.

In order to characterize the martial-erotic leader of the E-Anna side, we will use the acronym BDMB for Big Dick Macho Boss. We deliberately insist on using the poetics of modern thuggish English to express the visceral nature of what we are talking about here because polite-academic modern English is too Kullaba-esque to be able to properly render what is at stake. Using this scale-neutral phrase and acronym has the additional advantage of not overly connoting the idea of a ruler, thus making it applicable to a wide range of characters, from street thugs to barbarian chieftains to petty kings to emperors.

div.head: 4.3. The Red and the Black
div.p: This analytical framework also fundamentally relies on the Girardian dichotomy between the red (overt, state-sponsored charismatic idolatry) and the black (covert, stealthy, structurally sequestered mimetic devotion). As the Middle East and Europe underwent systemic transitions toward the rigid orthodoxies of the Abrahamic faiths, the E-Anna dynamic of the sovereignty engine was structurally compelled to migrate from the red to the black. Although forcefully stripped of its overtly polytheistic iconography, the Ishtarian mechanism remained functionally indispensable, persisting covertly within complex sociopolitical architectures. This subterranean continuity is starkly evident in institutions such as the medieval theology of the three orders (see Item 18 below) and the highly sequestered erotic-political dynamics of Islamic Kingship (Item 13). Despite this successful integration into the black, the historical continuum is periodically ruptured by charismatic flare-ups. During epochs of institutional fragility, the suppressed E-Anna energy frequently breaches its covert constraints, generating explosive red episodes of overt Ishtarian recrudescence (Items 19, 21, and 22).
